en: The Commentary on the Heart Sutra of the Perfection of Wisdom by Sengzhike.
It is said that this single work, the Heart Sutra, is the divine artifice of the sages and heroes of both the mundane and supramundane realms. Therefore—
One who grasps its essential intent governs the great trichiliocosm and rules over the world as if a clever child were tending sheep;
with the mere flick of a whip or a gesture, everything finds its proper place. To investigate its pivotal point, the single phrase "the five aggregates are all empty" is the very heart of this sutra.
Suppose there is a person here whose ambition lies in hearing the Way, yet who wishes to encompass both...
To abandon this "Book of Universal Goodness" while seeking something else is like setting out on a night journey and discarding one's torch; such a person is either a fool or a madman.
Generally speaking, the lack of clarity regarding the Way and the difficulty of governing the world both take root in the notion of self (*ātman*).
Once this notion of self is established, one feels joy upon seeing anything desirable; yet, if that which is desired does not satisfy one's ambitions, one becomes suddenly enraged.

Thus they become angry, and the celestial mechanism (tianji) is thereby blocked; likes and dislikes thereby become biased. Consequently, the primordial wisdom-light that is inherently present is completely buried and obscured.
Observing this in daily life, love and hatred battle within the spirit-mansion (lingtai), while emotional consciousnesses float and sink amidst honor and disgrace.
Observing this through the lens of past and present, one sees the mutual conflict of the Seven Hegemons and Five Barons.
As for the successes and failures of the Han, Tang, Song, Yuan, and other dynasties, even those that were entirely excellent and those that were not cannot be compared on the same footing.

Yet, when it comes to the fact that without martiality there would be chaos and the state could not be stabilized, and without wisdom the nation could not be preserved—in short, none of these transcend the mark of selfhood (*ātman*).
Consequently, true nature becomes daily obscured, while delusive thoughts become increasingly dense, and innate simplicity...
As the ways of the world decline day by day, it is said: "To govern a state with wisdom is to be a thief to that state; to have a self in governing people and things is to be their enemy.
Although a thief and an enemy may be bestowed by one's own parents upon their child, they will certainly not be able to carry out [the parents' intent];

not only will they be unable to carry it out, they will surely turn against them with hostile eyes and attack them. Thus, the Tathāgata knows that the poison of the *ātman*-view (*ātmagrāha*) pervades the world.
The harm is so great that within a single thought-moment, one opens up form and mind; from form and mind, one opens up the five aggregates (*skandhas*);
from the objects of form, one opens up the twelve bases (*āyatanas*); and from the five aggregates, one further opens up the eighteen elements (*dhātus*).

Thus, sentient beings come to realize that both attachment to the body and attachment to the mind are fundamentally rooted in the mark of self (*ātman*), and that the root of this mark of self arises from ignorance (*avidyā*).

Because each member of the chain conditions the next and arises through the characteristics of suffering and its origin, one who penetrates the source from which ignorance arises finds that the self-nature is naturally luminous;
one who penetrates that matter and mind lack intrinsic nature finds that not even a single thought-moment can be apprehended;

one who penetrates that the five aggregates lack intrinsic nature finds that matter and mind likewise cannot be apprehended; and one who penetrates the source from which the twelve bases arise is like a skilled butcher carving meat.
When one has reached the state where the ox is no longer perceived as a whole ox, by observing the twelve *āyatanas* (bases), this present body likewise cannot be found as a whole.
One who understands how the eighteen *dhātus* (elements) arise knows that the two dharmas of form and mind are externally analyzed into the six objects (*viṣaya*),
internally analyzed into the six faculties (*indriya*), and in the interim, consist of the vividly manifest discernment of the present moment.
When the mind of knowing is further analyzed, it is divided into the six consciousnesses. Alas!

Were it not for the Great Benevolence and Deep Compassion of our Buddha, how could the root of the self-view, the basis of poisonous harm, and the defilement of manifold sufferings be easily uprooted or cleansed? Cleansing these defilements is like cold waves lapping against stones;
uprooting them is like a vajra shattering objects. If one laps at the stones incessantly, they will surely eventually be worn away; if one strikes with the vajra, they will surely be shattered.

That which has already been possessed must ultimately become empty, just as a stone is eventually worn through; when things are empty, the self is discarded. This is what is meant by: "If one part is impaired, both will surely be lost.
When both things and self are forgotten, the original mind naturally reveals itself; hence it is said: "The numinous light shines alone, utterly transcending the sense organs and their objects.
If this light is used to illuminate the transcendental world, the path of awakening can be ascended; if it illuminates the mundane world...
In this interval, the ancient Way may be restored; therefore, I say that the *Heart Sūtra* is a divine artifice for both the mundane and the supramundane.
Among the eight divisions of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, its titles comprise over six hundred fascicles; yet this sūtra alone, at six hundred characters, constitutes the crux of those magnificent texts.
Furthermore, the crux of this sūtra lies in the phrase: "Illuminating and seeing that the five aggregates are all empty."
These words are correct: "To perceive that the five aggregates are all empty" is further rooted in the two dharmas of form and mind;
the two dharmas of form and mind are further rooted in a sudden stirring of a single thought; and this sudden stirring of a single thought is further rooted in the true mind.
This true mind is originally pure and tranquil, fundamentally devoid of sense organs, objects, things, or self, standing alone prior to the five aggregates, utterly without anything [to grasp].

When a single thought stirs, its origin is such that even those of great wisdom and lofty insight, when asked about the source from which that stirring arises, are ultimately unable to provide an answer. I, too, have harbored doubts regarding this for a long time.
How could there be a Great Master capable of shattering these doubts? I would be content to offer my own flesh as a sacrifice.
The *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra* (End). The Master’s name was Zhēnkě;
his courtesy name was Daguān, and he later took the sobriquet Zǐbó. His ancestors were from Jùqū, and his father, Shěnlián, was the youngest son of the family who had long resided in Wújiāng.
When the Master was seventeen years old, he encountered Míngjué at Hùqiū and left the household life. II.
After receiving full ordination, he went to the capital to study under Chan Master Bianrong; later, he entered Lengyan Temple, where he restored the ruined Tripitaka collection.
On the seventeenth day of the twelfth month of the Gui-mao year of the Wanli era, he passed away at the age of sixty-one.
